doc.title: Paquito D'Rivera — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Adding Claudio Roditi to the quintet
summary: Through a Brazilian guitarist in the building, he met Roditi and added him as second horn instead of the percussionist.

story.theme_name: Who was in the band: naming sidemen and personnel
story.community_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel

blocks.x: This band that made the record and made the gig at Soundscape, did this become your regular band?

That became my regular band, yea. Uh, for a long time, until the Broadway with Dizzy and eh, I used to use in percussion, just to, I ask Claudio Roditi on the trumpet and trombone, I need an extra soloist with me, and I like the quintet, the classical Be-bop quintet is a form that I like the most. So, up the stairs there was another loft, up in the sixth floor, there was a guy called Diego Romero. He was a Brazilian guitarist and composer who had a lot of that.

Same building, on the sixth floor of the Dracula castle. So, I met this guy and he told me, you have to meet Claudio Roditi; he’s a great trumpet player from Brazil and on those days, I understand that Claudio was planning to go back to Brazil because he didn’t have enough gigs here. So, I mention to Diego Romero that I was looking for an extra horn in the group, and I mention that, “You have to listen to Claudio Roditi; I mean he’s fantastic” He mix Brazilian music with Jazz very well, and I was in love with Brazilian music for many years. So, Claudio
was a vehicle to help me in the front line, and also to learn more about the Brazilian music. So, he, he came to my band.
You expanded the band to a quintet?
Well, it wasn’t a quintet with the percussionist.
So you used Claudio instead of percussion—
